headline: Heard update on automated trash collection pilot, PAYT bag compliance cameras, and food waste collection; approved April 28 minutes.
summary: Staff reported that the automated collection rollout is running smoothly, with about 7,000 carts dispatched. Cameras that check PAYT bag use estimate compliance at 90 to 95 percent, and staff plans to start outreach with postcards before any fines.
decisions: Approved the minutes of the April 28, 2026 meeting, with a typo correction on page 4. The minutes passed unanimously.
Consensus that staff should give a report reviewing the pilot, perhaps in a December timeframe.

decision_titles: Staff report on automated collection pilot
plain_text:
Solid Waste Advisory Committee Meeting 
 
10/6/26 
4:30 PM 
 
Members: 
 
Chair: Councilor Brent Todd     
 
Councilor Mark Davie     
 
Councilor Aislinn Kalob      
 
Councilor Judith Kurtz      
 
Councilor Jim Schlosser        
 
Councilor Kris Schultz      
 
Eric Steinhauser       
 
Reagan Bissonnette     
 
Carol Foss       
 
Linda Zollo     
 
Taylor Hall        
 
Guests:  
 
Michael Paine – Belmont Region Manager – Casella  
 
Tony Belanger – Strategic Account Manager - Casella 
 
Staff: 
 
Jeff Hoadley –General Services Director 
 
Marco Philippon –General Services Deputy Director  
 
Adam Clark – Administration Division Manager 
 
Angelina Zulkic – Communications Coordinator
At 4:30 PM, Chairman Todd called the meeting to order noting that a quorum was present. He thanked 
the committee for convening again to consult on what has been a busy summer for Staff and that he 
looked forward to hearing tonight’s presentation.   
 
The first order of business was approval of the minutes from the last SWAC meeting held on April 28th, 
2026.  With the correction of a typo on page 4, the minutes passed unanimously. 
 
With that, Chairman Todd turned the floor over to Staff from General Services.  Adam Clark from GSD 
would do the evening’s presentation.   
 
Mr. Clark started with an overview of the agenda.  Staff looks at the transition to automated collection 
in two ways; first is the operational side of things, meaning the cart 
deliveries/collections/logistics/service of the pilot, while the second is from a PAYT perspective, 
essentially how operations are funded.  He indicated he would close out the evening with updates on a 
few other items.   
 
Mr. Clark indicated he is incredibly proud of how the rollout has gone.  It has been widely well received 
by residents.  Carts began deploying in mid-June which led to a VERY BUSY 6- or 8-week period where 
cart size changes, missed locations and extra containers were dispatched.  An additional period of 
capturing and verifying that cart data in a database was conducted. At present, there are approximated 
7,000 carts dispatched at approximately 3,500 stops.  Mr. Clark thanked GSD staff members and Casella 
employees for the successful rollout. 
 
The presentation continued onto overviews of how operations are running smoothly.  Driver training is 
complete and has been successful, adjustments on the truck have been made to maximize efficiency 
(ram pressure).  Again, Mr. Clark spoke about the overwhelmingly positive reception from residents, 
starting with the delivery crews but continuing through the “cleanup phase” and onto routine 
operations. 
 
Mr. Clark wanted to explain to the committee “what’s happening when you see manual collection of 
automated bins?” He explained that, every day there are 3 or 4 trucks steadfastly servicing their own 
routes, however, unknown volumes at the curb can make the truck “pack out” or get filled before their 
assigned route is done or perhaps something needs attention on the truck and the truck must leave the 
assigned route. 
 
In those cases, other trucks from the other routes will “swarm” to the assigned route of the filled truck 
to finish that route so as to be the most efficient.  That is the art of it. While it would be great if 
everything went according to plan always, it doesn’t always happen and that is why we sometimes will 
see manual trucks servicing the automated route. 
 
The presentation continued; Amy Ouellette from the Engineering Department built our GIS tool which 
was a planning lifesaver. We must continue to plan using this tool as we move forward.  Absent that, we 
would have had a very different rollout, he stated. Councilor Schlosser echoed the importance of this 
tool. 
 
The “cleanup phase”, that being the phase where post-delivery size adjustments and correcting for 
unidentified stops, took much longer than anticipated. While the City was very clear about getting the
word out on requesting size adjustment in an initial pre-delivery window, many, many, many people 
wanted size adjustments after delivery. 
 
Thanks to a last-minute order of “extra” containers, the City was able to satisfy ALL requests, which is 
remarkable, He would really like us to look at how we can prompt the requests in the requested pre-
delivery window better as while they were able to satisfy all of the requests received, that may not 
always be the case based on limited inventory and supply. 
 
Another thing learned was that the data from Engineering especially around condos and mixed-use 
properties is probably the weakest in terms of accuracy.  Extra attention needs to be paid here in the 
future, especially as the project approaches the city center. 
 
Last reflection is just that where necessary, Staff was able to spend extra time/accommodate some 
areas that needed extra attention in a way that he thinks ends up making a better final outcome. 
 
Mr. Clark then gave a brief overview on the future planning efforts.  He indicated that given what they 
consider to be great success in the rollout, and upon consultation with City Staff and the folks from 
Casella, there are a few things that need to considered as they move forward. First is simply perhaps 
having waves of communications so that Staff can better manage call volumes in the office when they 
send out postcards.  They tend to generate a lot of questions and require a lot of Staff time so perhaps 
they can cut cycles in half and stagger them to help with that. 
 
The second thing is that they have had some very preliminary meetings where they recognize that 
because they have been so successful in distribution and operations thus far, they think it may not be 
possible to maintain that standard by doing the rest of the City in just one more phase given the number 
of households. 
 
In recognition of that, preliminary talks about pivoting to a 3-phase approach so that the rollout remains 
orderly and successful have occurred.  Generally, it has been discussed that perhaps converting the 
remaining rural areas in the second phase in 2028 as per the original plan and then following that up 
with a planned rollout in the city center was a good idea and adjustment in the pilot. 
 
Staff believes this is prudent because it allows for a better chance of continued success given the 
numbers of households but stay tuned, Staff expects to return here with more details on what that 
would look like in early 2027 though.   
 
With that, Mr. Clark turned to PAYT compliance, as you recall, cameras have been installed on the 
automated collection truck to verify compliance with the PAYT bag requirement in an effort to maintain 
that revenue source. 
 
That system is currently up and running and after a short delay in installation in getting the computer 
itself, “systems learning” and data gathering phases have occurred per previous discussions.   
 
The system exceeds everyone’s expectations.  The images are clear, the cart data is loaded in the 
system, the GPS data is functional and accurate.  All in all, it is very impressive and perhaps most 
importantly, this system could potentially allow the City to preserve is its PAYT system/policy.
Within the system, Mr. Clark noted, are various attributes which allow for “high confidence” when 
identifying non-compliance.  Those attributes include, GPS location. Street-view images and cart 
numbers as well as the hopper footage. It is very important to Staff to “get it right” as outreach begins. 
 
Compliance to date is very good, estimated at north of 90%. Perhaps as high as 95%.  He then began 
sharing images from the system starting with a map of so called “service events” or collections. It 
represents a typical day.   
 
The next series of images illustrated what images that include the use of purple PAYT bags look like.  The 
images show a hopper with purple bags. Then came an image showing non-compliance.  The bags are 
not purple and are therefore what the system is designed to identify.   
 
He then illustrated so called “heat maps” of non-compliance.  These will be helpful in steering outreach 
campaigns or cart inspection efforts which the Committee has discussed previously.   
 
Moving forwards, Staff is preparing what the outreach campaign will look like.  The campaign would 
likely start with postcards and not fines or discontinuation of service, leaving those as protentional 
recourses down the line for repeat offenders if the Committee so chooses.  This will allow the City to see 
how effective these tools are in addressing the issue.   
 
Example images were then shown of a draft postcard.  There was discussion of the complications of 
reaching tenants vs property owners which is complicated by the fact that there is no way for the City to 
verify which cart is used by which unit in a multifamily property.   
 
Subsequent campaigns could be crafted around this nuance in a follow-up campaign that addressed the 
issue at a property more broadly than a specific incident. 
 
The proposed postcard includes the following elements; 
• Oops. 
• Picture of non-compliance. 
• Under that picture is the address of the service event.  
• The property owner address (the mailing address). 
• PAYT Bags are required. 
• Commentary on bags helping cover the costs of collection and disposal. 
• Please use PAYT bags. 
• QR code for more info. 
• A reference to a continuum of enforcement which was put together for the pilot rules 
suggesting that other enforcement measures may come 
 
Mr. Clark continued that with a few tweaks the City will be ready to execute however, it would be wise 
for the City to first put together a policy around the use of the system.  This could include hitting on such 
topics as identifying non-compliance, privacy and data management considerations.   
 
Deputy City Solicitor Danielle Sakowski has offered to come join the Committee to discuss these issues 
in November.  Mr. Clark indicated they would work together to frame a draft policy in anticipation of 
that if the group desired. Dates could be discussed at the end of the meeting.
Then before wrapping up compliance, Mr. Clark highlighted that data including PAYT bag sales, tonnage, 
heat maps and ultimately PAYT compliance metrics would be used as the pilot continues to inform the 
conversation. 
 
Mr. Clark then reminded the Committee that they had been interested in a Council Report in the past 
and he asked what form that would take and when.  The consensus was generally that a Staff report 
reviewing the story shared this evening would be great, perhaps in a December timeframe.  Mr. Clark 
understood the direction.   
 
Wrapping up the presentation, Mr. Clark then gave brief updates on two topics; 
 
Food Waste Collection which is on track.  A needed NHDES permit modification would be submitted 
shortly.  Further planning efforts would commence with a meeting with Renewal Compost on 10/20.  
The City will explore any potential grant opportunities and be back with more info for everyone before 
the collection starts.   
 
Bagged Leaf Collection funding was cut as part of FY27 budget deliberations.  Bulk collections remain 
unchanged.  Residents may drop bagged leaves in less than pickup-truck load quantities at the Earth 
Material Recycling Center/Raymond’s on Fort Eddy Road for no fee. 
 
The committee then deliberated on the path forward.  Program planning efforts would continue with an 
effort to dive into communication strategy and more info on transition phases to be discussed in early 
2027.  
 
The committee also discussed convening in November with the Deputy City Solicitor on PAYT 
compliance policy matters.  Mr. Clark would confirm. 
 
Outreach material development would continue. 
 
Mr. Clark lastly shared updates on looking into how other municipalities fund their solid waste 
operations, while detailing recent conversations with the City of Dover, NH which is transitioning to 
automated collection and abandoning their PAYT program, deciding instead to put collection back on 
the General Fund to pay for.  As budget deliberations in that City continue, all should watch for 
developments.   
 
With the Conclusion of that, Chairman Todd wanted to take the opportunity to thank Staff for their hard 
work and dedication in planning and executing phase 1 of the transition.  The committee echoed this 
sentiment. Then at 5:55 PM, Chairman Todd accepted a motion by Councilor Kalob to adjourn, which 
was seconded by Councilor Schulz. The committee passed the motion and adjourned.












Minutes prepared by Adam Clark.
